title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
summary: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

title: Doublecortin compacts the microtubule lattice through a DC1-dependent mechanism
summary: Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule-associated protein essential for neuronal migration during brain development, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its function on the microtubule remain incompletely understood. Here we show that DCX compacts the microtubule lattice, with the DC1 domain serving as the main driver of lattice compaction. Using in vitro reconstitution, optical trapping, and molecular dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that although DCX preferentially binds compacted microtubule lattices, it can also bind expanded lattices and remodel them by inducing ~2-3 [A] compaction at interdimer interfaces. This compaction stiffens microtubules and inhibits kinesin-1 and TAT1 binding. The DC1 domain is necessary for lattice compaction, whereas DC2 is dispensable for this function. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that DC1 binding induces shearing and hinge motions that stabilize compacted conformations absent from apo tubulin, thereby reducing lattice heterogeneity. Our findings establish DCX as a bona fide microtubule remodeler and provide a molecular framework for understanding how DCX contributes to neuronal development through the control of microtubule lattice conformation.

title: Parametric and AI-Assisted Design of Right-Handed Four-Helix Coiled Coils
summary: Right-handed, antiparallel -helical coiled coils are rare in nature and remain challenging targets for de novo protein design. Here, we combined parametric backbone generation with deep-learning-based sequence design and structure prediction to systematically explore this underrepresented region of coiled-coil structural space. We compared three ProteinMPNN design strategies: repeat-constrained homotetramer design, unconstrained homotetramer design, and unconstrained heterotetramer design. Removing strict sequence repeat constraints increased the fraction of designs satisfying structural confidence and topology criteria approximately sixfold, from 0.44% to 2.80%, while simultaneous optimization of two distinct peptide sequences yielded a success rate of 3.04%. Selected designs were evaluated for assembly using a split-luciferase complementation assay in mammalian cells, followed by circular dichroism spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations. Five of six experimentally characterized designs exhibited predominantly -helical structures, with apparent melting temperatures ranging from 55.2 to 72.5 {degrees}C. The crystal structure of the most stable design, Heteromer-2, determined at 1.92 [A] resolution, confirmed the intended right-handed, antiparallel architecture, with a backbone RMSD of only 0.45 [A] relative to the computational model. Our findings establish a strategy for designing noncanonical coiled-coil architectures by combining precise parametric control of backbone geometry with flexible, AI-assisted sequence optimization.

title: The C-terminal region of interferon-γ mediates evolutionarily tunable membrane interaction
summary: Interferon-{gamma} (IFN-{gamma}) is a key cytokine orchestrating innate and adaptive immunity, yet the functional significance of its highly basic C-terminal region remains poorly understood. Here, we combine evolutionary, biophysical, cellular, and computational approaches to uncover the membrane-interacting properties of this region across vertebrate IFN-{gamma} orthologs. We show that the previously described conserved KRKR motif is embedded within a broader cationic region that is highly diverse in fish but progressively reduced in terrestrial tetrapods. Molecular dynamics simulations and experiments using large unilamellar vesicles reveal preferential interactions with anionic membranes. Furthermore, all tested IFN-{gamma}-derived peptides associate with U-2 OS cells, with the olive flounder-derived peptide displaying exceptionally strong cellular association and cell penetration, markedly exceeding that of the canonical cell-penetrating peptide R9. Together, our findings identify the IFN-{gamma} C-terminus as an evolutionarily diverse, membrane-interacting module with pronounced cell-penetrating properties in certain fish orthologs, revealing an unexpected functional dimension of this conserved immune protein.

title: Activation of the bridge-like lipid transfer protein Atg2 by Atg1-mediated phosphorylation
summary: Bridge-like lipid transfer proteins (BLTPs) have emerged as major contributors to lipid flux and thus cellular organization. BLTPs harbor a hydrophobic channel connecting two membranes to enable the bulk flow of lipids between them. The regulation of BLTPs is incompletely understood. Employing in vitro reconstitution, molecular dynamics simulations, and cell biology, we discovered that the BLTP Atg2, which mediates lipid transfer during autophagosome biogenesis, is activated by the Atg1 kinase. Atg1 phosphorylates two serines in the N-terminal region of Atg2. This triggers membrane binding and is predicted to open the channel for lipid transfer. The Atg1 kinase complex is localized to the endoplasmic reticulum in part through binding of its Atg13 subunit to the VAP protein Scs2. Phosphorylated Atg2 can subsequently establish contacts with Atg9 vesicles. Our study delineates a pathway for the Atg1 kinase mediated activation of the BLTP Atg2 to promote membrane contact site formation and lipid flux.

title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
summary: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

title: Thermodynamic, Kinetic, and Structural Basis of Polyspecificity in the Malaria Sugar Transporter PfHT1
summary: The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum relies on the polyspecific sugar transporter PfHT1 for survival in diverse nutrient environments, making the molecular basis of its polyspecificity a potential avenue for antimalarial drug discovery. However, the structural, thermodynamic and kinetic basis of the emergence of polyspecificity in membrane transporters are not established in literature. Despite advances in AI for protein engineering, the design of selective/promiscuous membrane transporter proteins remains challenging as it requires connecting substrate recognition to the energetics of the transport cycle. Here, we examine the molecular origins of polyspecificity in PfHT1 transporter using molecular dynamics simulations of substrate transport and experimental validation of the key residues that tune specificity. From a structural viewpoint, we hypothesize that polyspecific membrane transporter contains flexible structural elements that could reshape the binding pocket in a substrate-dependent manner. For PfHT1, the cracking of the extracellular helix TM7b allows flexible reshaping of the binding pocket similar to the promiscuous enzymes. The thermodynamic signature of polyspecificity emerges in the form of the substrate dependent stabilization of transport-competent states. From a kinetic perspective, this stabilization asymmetrically alters transition kinetics and channels the flux through diverse conformational pathways that facilitate the conformational transitions from outward to inward facing states. To investigate the contribution of the underlying interaction network to sugar specificity, we used graph-attention learning to prioritize mutant transporters with distinct substrate preferences. Distinct glucose- and fructose-dependent growth phenotypes identify positions with differential effects on sugar utilization, providing functional evidence relevant to substrate specificity within the polyspecific transporter. Together, these findings support a mechanism in which structural, thermodynamic and kinetics observables connect polyspecificity to conformational energetics, kinetics, and structural plasticity.

title: Machine learning cross-platform proteomic imputation enables protein quality scoring and replication of epidemiological associations
summary: High-throughput affinity-based proteomics has advanced biomedical research, yet fundamental, persistent discordance between mainstream platforms (SomaScan and Olink) routinely undermines the replication of findings. This platform-driven non-replication complicates downstream biological validation and biomarker prioritization. Here, we develop a machine learning-based framework for cross-platform protein value imputation to navigate this translational bottleneck. Using paired proteomic data measured by both SomaScan and Olink from 5,325 participants of the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, we developed models to impute cross-platform measurements and applied them to two independent and demographically distinct cohorts (Cardiovascular Health Study [N=3,171] and UK Biobank [UKB; N=41,405]) to evaluate downstream replication. Our bidirectional model 1) established an imputation performance-based protein fidelity index, validated against gold-standard / orthogonal measurements (ELISA and Simoa/Quanterix in Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study [ARIC, N=101] and Nurses' Health Study [NHS, N=54], and published mass spectrometry data), 2) enabled imputation of platform-exclusive protein measurements, and 3) facilitated calibration of overlapping proteins. We demonstrate the utility of this framework through three applications: 1) fidelity-informed analyses enhanced the replication of biomarker discovery, 2) recovery of SomaScan signals that were previously inaccessible in UKB's original Olink measurements, and 3) improved replication performance for overlapping proteins. Our study offers a translational roadmap that helps researchers identify more confident cross-platform measurements to support replication efforts, identify potential assays warranting future optimization, and distinguish proteins where biological signal likely dominates platform-specific measurement.

title: Conserved Vulnerability, Local Tunability: How Binding Proteins Read Ligand Fluorination
summary: While rare in nature, fluorinated compounds are ubiquitous in synthetic chemicals ranging from pharmaceuticals to agrochemicals, yet how proteins recognize these anthropogenic molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we use three structurally and evolutionarily divergent solute-binding proteins (SBPs) specific for short-chain dicarboxylic acids as a comparative model system to dissect the principles governing protein-fluorocompound recognition. X-ray crystal structures reveal that each SBP uses a distinct binding mode, ranging from backbone-mediated to side-chain-dominated hydrogen bonding. Despite their structural divergence, ITC shows that all three proteins exhibit a conserved vulnerability upon binding perfluorinated ligands: binding affinity drops up to 80-fold, or is abolished, across all three proteins regardless of fold or binding mode. In contrast, sensitivity to partial fluorination is locally tunable, with one protein even binding a fluorinated ligand more tightly than its non-fluorinated counterpart. Using X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics simulations, and site-directed mutagenesis, we show that aromatic residues positioned near the ligand contribute to this tunability, capable of either penalizing or favoring fluorinated ligands. Together, these findings establish that ligand-fluorination sensitivity reflects a conserved chemical vulnerability layered with locally tunable, structurally encoded selectivity, providing a roadmap for predicting and engineering protein recognition of fluorinated compounds.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Generative Models for Capturing Topological Features in Brain Structural Connectivity Matrices
summary: Structural connectivity (SC) data are crucial for brain network analysis, but SC-based machine learning often suffers from limited data availability, hindering model generalization and robustness. Although data augmentation using deep generative models has attracted increasing attention, it remains unclear how different models capture the complex topological features of SC data. To clarify the model-specific generative characteristics of deep generative models for ROI-level weighted SC matrix generation, this study compares three representative models: variational autoencoder (VAE), Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP), and denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM). We systematically evaluated these models using both synthetic datasets as diagnostic benchmarks to isolate model-specific biases in reproducing graph properties and two real-world SC datasets. Generation quality was assessed using graph-theoretic metric comparisons and visual inspection of the generated adjacency matrices across four training runs. For the empirical SC datasets, we also evaluated inter-subject variability and sample diversity. WGAN-GP performed consistently across synthetic datasets and achieved the strongest results on most metrics for both SC datasets, most closely reproducing variability and diversity. VAE captured average characteristics but underestimated sample variability. DDPM reproduced stochastic connection patterns but struggled with coordinate-specific patterns and run-to-run consistency. Despite WGAN-GP's balanced performance, each model had distinct strengths and limitations, emphasizing the need to consider relevant graph properties when comparing generative models. All models struggled to reproduce strict global constraints, such as planarity. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating structural constraints alongside statistical similarity and accounting for graph-specific properties when developing generative models.

title: Predicting conformational changes induced by biomolecular interactions
summary: Biomolecular interactions trigger structural changes of protein complexes essential for cellular signaling, regulation, and drug action. Modern co-folding models can now generate detailed structures of multi-component complexes directly from sequence. However, recent evaluations reveal that they frequently fail to capture specific conformational states induced by a ligand or partner. Here, we show that explicitly modeling the structural transition from an unbound to a bound state, rather than generating the bound complex alone, better resolves these interaction-induced states. Our generative learning framework, K-Fold, transforms independently predicted unbound component priors into an assembled complex through an ultrafast diffusion bridge, operating entirely without multiple sequence alignments. By eliminating co-evolutionary dependencies, K-Fold accurately recovers non-coevolved interfaces in antibody-antigen and targeted-degrader complexes, as well as ligand-directed regulatory states in GPCRs and kinases. Furthermore, by coupling this diffusion bridge with diverse monomeric equilibrium ensembles, K-Fold provides a computationally tractable foundation for sampling complex multi-state landscapes without retraining. These results demonstrate that formulating molecular assembly as an explicit structural transition moves structure prediction beyond static geometries toward capturing biomolecular dynamics.

title: Quantum-assisted genomic prediction of blast resistance in rice (Oryza sativa L.) using SNP and haplotype representations
summary: Rice blast caused by Magnaporthe oryzae threatens rice production, and genomic prediction may accelerate identification of resistant germplasm. We evaluated classical machine-learning and simulated quantum-kernel models for binary and three-class prediction of leaf blast (BL) and panicle blast (PB) resistance in 204 rice accessions with 2,120 repeated phenotypic observations. Models used 328,597 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), 104,068 phased haplotypes, or 49,451 unphased haplotypes. Binary prediction outperformed three-class prediction. The highest binary macro-F1 scores were 0.87 for BL and 0.73 for PB. Phased and unphased haplotypes reduced predictor dimensionality by 68.3% and 85.0%, respectively, while retaining broadly comparable performance. Quantum support vector classification achieved competitive results in selected binary tasks but did not consistently exceed the strongest classical models. These findings establish a benchmark for SNP- and haplotype-based prediction of rice blast resistance and for evaluation of quantum machine learning in crop genomics.

title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
summary: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

title: Machine Learning-Assisted Raman Spectroscopy for Quantitative Prediction of Multicomponent Mixtures
summary: Machine Learning (ML)-assisted Raman spectroscopy that can efficiently analyze molecularly specific fingerprints is well suited for quantitative analysis of complex chemical mixtures. However, developing accurate predictive ML models for multicomponent systems remains difficult because collecting sufficient experimental calibration data is slow, expensive, and limited. In this work, we present a ML-assisted Raman spectroscopy framework for predicting the quantitative composition of multicomponent lipid mixtures (consisting of 15 lipids). To reduce the experimental burden of generating extensive multicomponent spectral datasets, we computationally constructed a large spectral library using experimentally measured pure-component Raman spectra from 15 lipids, including triglycerides, medium- and long-chain fatty acids, and fatty acid methyl and ethyl esters. Mixture compositions were sampled across a constrained compositional space and used to generate training spectra from weighted combinations of the pure component spectra. Experimentally prepared mixtures were then used to evaluate the model under real measurement conditions. To reduce the mismatch between library-generated spectra and experimental mixture spectra, a linear correction strategy was applied to account for systematic spectral differences caused by mixing effects, intermolecular interactions, and measurement variability. The corrected experimental spectra were then used for concentration prediction with an uncertainty-aware workflow. The compositions of the 15 lipid mixtures were successfully predicted using the ML model trained solely on a simulated dataset, achieving R^2 values exceeding 0.95 for each lipid. By combining scalable, library-based model training with experimental validation on physical multicomponent mixtures, this approach minimizes the need for exhaustive calibration datasets while maintaining high quantitative accuracy. The proposed framework offers a practical path for quantitative Raman analysis of chemical mixtures and can easily be extended to quality control applications across the food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and chemical industries.

title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning
summary: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.

title: Investigating the critical role of serine in antimicrobial peptide binding to lipopolysaccharide
summary: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a major component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, is a potent endotoxin responsible for triggering severe host immune responses and sepsis. Understanding the atomic-level mechanisms governing how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) recognize and neutralize LPS is essential for designing effective anti-endotoxin therapeutics. Here, we present an in silico investigation of the single-molecule interaction between Escherichia coli O111:B4 LPS and the cationic antimicrobial peptide GL13K, alongside two single-point mutants at position 9 (GL13KS9A and GL13KS9T), using all-atom molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Consistent with experimental trends, mutating SER9 into alanine significantly alters peptide binding affinity to LPS. Surpisingly, removal of the polar character of serine leads to substantial changes in the interaction of the N-terminus with LPS via the loss of hydrogen bonding to stabilize a hook shape at the C-terminal end. In specific, while wild-type GL13K exhibits the strongest unbinding free-energy barrier, the S9A substitution changes the conformational landscape in such a way as to redirect the peptide's N-terminus from lipid A toward the core oligosaccharide and substantially reduces the unbinding barrier, whereas S9T maintains an similar affinity. Our work demonstrates the effects of distal mutations even in peptides on their binding and lays important groundwork for the development of peptide-based LPS inhibitors.
